title: Why LEDs Emit Light & How They're Made – From Physics to Production

segments.label: Cold Open: The Light‑Switch Inside a Chip
segments.text: What if a single chip could turn electricity into visible light? You’ll hear how a tiny semiconductor does exactly that, and why it matters for everything that glows around you. Imagine a diode no bigger than a grain of sand, yet it can shine bright enough to replace a tiny indicator lamp. How does a piece of silicon manage that? When current flows, electrons crash into holes inside the semiconductor. That collision releases energy as photons—tiny packets of light. The color you see depends on the band‑gap energy each material requires. Early versions only emitted faint red or invisible infrared, but today they span infrared, visible, and ultraviolet wavelengths. You might wonder why such a small part can be used in traffic signals, aircraft lights, and even camera flashes. The answer lies in their ability to convert electricity directly into light without a filament. This makes them perfect for fast‑switching applications and modern displays. Stay with me, because next we’ll explore the physics that lets electrons become photons.

segments.label: From Electrons to Photons: The Core Physics
segments.text: What makes that tiny chip flash? Electrons rush in and find empty spots called holes. When an electron fills a hole, it drops to a lower energy level and spits out a photon – that’s electroluminescence. The photon’s color isn’t random; it matches the energy gap the electron crossed. A red LED’s band‑gap is about 1.8 eV, so the photon carries that much energy. A blue LED needs roughly 3 eV, so you must push a higher voltage to bridge the gap. Why does the chip need extra voltage for blue? Because the band‑gap is larger, demanding more electrical potential. The semiconductor itself has a high refractive index, like looking into water. Light would get trapped unless we coat the surface with special optical layers and shape the die to funnel photons outward. Those coatings act like tiny anti‑reflection lenses, and the die’s angled facets act as mirrors, steering the light out of the crystal. Want to see how we get pure white from a single blue chip? That’s the next trick, where we blend colors inside the package.

segments.label: A Century of Discovery: From Carborundum Glow to Nobel Prize
segments.text: Ever wonder who first saw a crystal glow like a tiny streetlamp? In 1906 Henry Round watched silicon‑carbide crystals flash yellow‑green when he applied a voltage. That flicker was the first hint that a solid could turn electricity into light. How did a Soviet tinkerer pick up that spark? Oleg Losev built the very first silicon‑carbide LED in 1927, turning the lab curiosity into a real device. You might think the story ends there, but the glow was still infrared and barely visible. What changed the game in the ’60s? Texas Instruments engineers patented efficient near‑infrared gallium‑arsenide LEDs in 1962, proving a diode could emit light reliably enough for commercial interest. Fast forward to the early 1990s: three Japanese scientists—Shuji Nakamura, Hiroshi Amano and Isamu Akasaki—crafted the first practical blue LEDs. Their blue chips finally let you mix colors into white light. Their breakthrough earned the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics. Curious how that blue chip becomes the white glow in your lamp? Stay tuned, because the next trick mixes colors inside the package.

segments.label: How White Light Is Made: Phosphor vs. RGB
segments.text: What if the tiny blue chip in your lamp were a paintbrush? You coat it with a thin layer of cerium‑doped YAG phosphor. Part of the blue light turns yellow. That shift is called a Stokes shift – the photons lose a bit of energy and emerge at a longer wavelength. Why does that matter? Your eye sees yellow far better than blue, so the same power looks 3‑5 × brighter. The result is a phosphor‑converted white LED – the workhorse of high‑intensity lighting. Another route mixes separate red, green, and blue LEDs. You can tune the exact shade of white, even push it cool or warm. The catch? You need extra circuitry to balance the three colors, and each emits a slightly different pattern. Look from the side and the hue can change – a color‑angle shift. That complexity makes RGB white LEDs rarer in mass lighting. Because phosphor coating is simple and cheap, manufacturers favor it for most bright lamps. You get a single blue InGaN chip, a thin phosphor film, and a white glow without extra drivers. The next trick shows how factories squeeze even more efficiency out of that tiny chip.

segments.label: Manufacturing Tricks that Boost Efficiency
segments.text: What if the chip itself could be printed on a cheap silicon slab instead of a pricey sapphire crystal? GaN‑on‑silicon 200‑mm wafers do exactly that, swapping out the expensive sapphire and opening the door to bigger factories. The industry even forecast that by 2020, forty percent of all GaN LEDs will come from those silicon sheets. Now picture a high‑power LED crammed with current. It can push a staggering 300 W per square centimeter. That’s bright enough to blind a moth, but only if the heat disappears fast. Without a heat‑sink the device burns out in seconds – a literal flash‑in‑the‑pan. Why do manufacturers obsess over these numbers? Because Haitz’s law promises exponential gains, and the record books prove it. In 2009 the CREE XP‑G hit 105 lumens per watt. A year later Nichia’s 19 series topped 140 lumens per watt. Those jumps aren’t magic; they’re the result of tighter wafers, hotter chips, and relentless engineering. So how do factories keep squeezing light from a chip that’s already scorching? The answer lies in the next manufacturing sleight of hand…

segments.label: Payoff: Why LEDs Light Our World Today
segments.text: What powers the glow in your TV remote? A tiny LED, humming on a few volts. You’re probably holding one right now, sending invisible infrared pulses to your couch. Those same chips sit in car headlights, flashing on highways, and line greenhouses where seedlings stretch toward artificial sunrise. How can something so small replace a bulky bulb? Because LEDs sip electricity. An incandescent bulb burns a hundred watts to give off the same light a LED delivers with a fraction of that power. Less power means less heat wasted as hot air. You’ll notice your phone charger stays cool, not scorching like an old lamp. LEDs also outlast their filament cousins, lasting far longer before dimming. Their solid‑state design survives drops, vibrations, and temperature swings that would shatter a glass bulb. You might wonder why you still see LED strips on a wall plug instead of a wall socket. The answer is voltage: LEDs prefer low‑voltage DC, not raw AC. Seoul Semiconductor solved that by engineering LEDs that light on each half‑cycle of AC, delivering roughly 40 lumens per watt without a separate driver.
